items.new: "Drink and pass!" he cried, handing the heavy, full flagon to the nearest seaman. "The crew alone drinks now. Pass it round! Short sips — long swallows, men. It's hot as Satan's hoof. Good, good — it goes round well. It spirals into you. It forks out at the serpent-snapping eye. Well done — nearly drained. That way it went, this way it comes. Hand it back — here's a hollow! Men, you are like the years: brimming life is gulped and gone. Steward, refill!"

items.reason: "Yonder" is the one leftover archaic word in the soliloquy; the rest of Ahab's elevated grammar is modernized.
items.new: Out there, at the ever-brimming goblet's rim, the warm waves blush like wine. The golden brow plumbs the blue. The diver sun — slowly dived from noon — goes down. My soul mounts up! She tires of her endless hill. Is, then, the crown too heavy that I wear? This Iron Crown of Lombardy. Yet it is bright with many a gem. I, the wearer, cannot see its distant flashing — but I darkly feel that I wear something that dazzlingly confounds. It is iron — that I know — not gold. It is cracked, too — I feel it. The jagged edge chafes me so, my brain seems to beat against the solid metal. Yes, a steel skull, mine — the kind that needs no helmet in the most brain-battering fight!

items.new: As for those who had previously heard of the White Whale and then happened to see him — at first, almost every one of them had lowered for him as boldly and fearlessly as for any other sperm whale. But eventually, such catastrophes resulted from these attacks — not just sprained wrists and ankles, broken limbs, or devouring amputations, but fatalities of the deadliest kind — that these repeated, disastrous defeats, all piling their terrors onto Moby Dick, had gone far toward shaking the courage of many brave hunters who later heard the story of the White Whale.

items.new: It is well known to both American and English whale ships, and was also placed on authoritative record years ago by Scoresby, that some whales captured far north in the Pacific have been found with the barbs of harpoons thrown in the Greenland seas still in their bodies. Nor can it be denied that in some of these cases it has been declared that the time between the two attacks could not have been very many days. Hence, by inference, some whalemen have believed that the Northwest Passage, so long a problem to man, was never a problem to the whale. So that here, in the real living experience of living men, the wonders told in old times of the inland Strello mountain in Portugal (near whose top there was said to be a lake in which the wrecks of ships floated up to the surface), and that still more wonderful story of the Arethusa fountain near Syracuse (whose waters were believed to have come from the Holy Land by an underground passage) — these fabulous tales are almost fully equaled by the realities of the whalemen.

items.new: But though this point is settled beyond dispute, how can any mortal account for it? To analyze it seems impossible. Can we, then, by citing some of those cases where this thing of whiteness — though for the time mostly or entirely stripped of all associations meant to make it fearful — is still found to work the same spell on us, however softened, hope to stumble upon some clue that leads us to the hidden cause we seek?

items.new: Why does the bare mention of Whitsuntide (the church season of Pentecost), to the man of untrained imagination who happens to be only loosely acquainted with the particular character of the day, marshal in his fancy such long, dreary, speechless processions of slow-pacing pilgrims, downcast and hooded with new-fallen snow? Or why, to the unread, unsophisticated Protestant of the Middle American States, does the passing mention of a White Friar or a White Nun call up such an eyeless statue in the soul?

items.new: It was the middle watch, in fair moonlight. The seamen were standing in a line stretching from one of the freshwater casks in the waist to the scuttlebutt (the drinking-water cask) near the taffrail. In this way they passed the buckets along to fill the scuttlebutt. Standing, for the most part, on the sacred ground of the quarter-deck, they were careful not to speak or shuffle their feet.
